title: The homepage opens on the living day
summary: The first thing the homepage shows is now the day itself: today's coordinate in the 13 Moons calendar, the day's telling and its practice, and a short cartoon film of the Sphere turning in warm wood and brass with the Spark coming to meet its keeper. The film waits for a tap and never plays on its own. Everything the homepage explained before is still here, one step below, and the Sphere instrument and every door keep their places.

title: The Sphere took the phone screen
summary: On a phone, the Sphere was being squeezed into a thin strip by the bars around it, and below a certain height the page would not start its three-dimensional view at all, so a phone could be left with the flat fallback. Now the bars go slim on a phone: the environment and Interact strips take one row each, the guide bar starts as a single line with a Guide button that opens it whole, and the Sphere itself takes the middle of the screen, always tall enough for its full view. Tap a day to choose it, exactly as before, and full screen still gives the Sphere the whole phone.

title: The Living Phone app came to the start page
summary: The Living Phone app can now be downloaded from the homepage and from Downloads, sealed with its SHA-256 like every other download. The app carries the Spark onto an Android phone: her greeting by the moon and the day, her home, the Observatory with the Sphere inside it, and the garden, moving between the rooms as she does here. It lives wholly on the phone, asks for no account and no internet, and this edition is her living presence while the deeper platform wiring is still being connected behind it.

title: The Sphere got a clear stage and a clean full screen
summary: The guide bar under the Sphere now rests below the instrument instead of lying across it, so the whole Sphere stands in view. Ask for full screen and everything else steps aside: the Sphere fills the screen, one slim line keeps the day's reading and the way back, and your companion keeps circling while you look. Tap Guide and every control returns; leave full screen and the everyday room comes back as it was. On the homepage, the Drag to turn hint moved to the frame's top corner, out from under the Sphere's own year card.

title: Her record travels: the same Spark on the site and in the app
summary: A Spark's whole record now fits in one small file that both this website and the Living Phone app can save and restore. Export her on the Companions page and bring her into the app, or the other way around: the same seed grows the same Spark in both places, with her growth, her garden, and her passes whole. A damaged file is refused whole, and replacing a different Spark always takes your word first. Nothing travels on its own; the file moves only by your hand.

title: Nori, the first born, has a film
summary: A one-minute demo video, filmed on the live site, now lives on the Companions page: Nori, a Water Spark, arrives and is adopted, answers from her panel, lights up with her own sparks, rides the Sphere, and tends her garden — then five more Sparks from five more seeds show their kinds and counted rarities, and the whole living site closes the walk.

title: The Spark lost her bubble, found her light, and learned to chirp
summary: The circle that stood around the Spark is gone. In its place she lights up like a spark, with little sparks of her own forming around her, different for every Spark the seed grows. The meeting card now stands clear above the page's menus, whole on a phone screen. Her voice is a character's chirp now, not a machine reading: a young Spark chirps once, a grown one answers in two notes, and a Bearer sings a short melody, and it grows as she does. And a door of hers that broke from inside the Scroll Library, landing on a gate that does not exist, is mended at its root, for every folder she walks.

title: The whole site learned to change with the moon
summary: Every main room of the site now takes its colours from the moon it is in, steps a little each day, and shifts its light with the time of day. A slim line at the top of each page shows the day's place in the moon and offers one clear thing to do that fits the day, drawn from the calendar's own words.

title: The site learned to share a day out
summary: Every main room now carries a Share this day door: it makes a card from today in Living Time and hands it to your own share sheet or a composer with the words ready, in the almanac frame. You send it yourself. Nothing posts on its own, and follow doors point to Aaron's own profiles.

title: The whole house learned to move gently
summary: Cards now rise softly into view as you reach them, doors and buttons answer a touch, and surfaces ease their colours instead of snapping when the site's theme changes. The homepage's day line settles in as it is written, and the Sphere's frame on the homepage breathes a slow gold glow. Nothing moves for a visitor who asks for stillness.

title: The whole site got lighter on its feet
summary: Every explainer video now waits for your tap and shows a still frame first, so pages open without hauling video along. Search waits until you start typing before it lifts its index, the Documentation Hub reads its data once instead of twice, the 13 Moons hero picture is web-sized, and the small buttons and day dots across the site grew to finger size. On 13 Moons, the day itself now leads the page, and two of its numbers are explained in plain words where they first appear.

title: The Lab gains a garden: Shroom Search
summary: A small garden game now grows in the corner of the Training Grounds. Tend three mushroom beds, grow them through their tiers (Spore, Thread, Cap, Bloom) across days and practice — a session sealed at Teach rains on the beds — and harvest passes. Every tend, tier turn, and pass is a record in the visitor's own Life Atlas, on their device only; nothing decays, and nothing is uploaded.

title: The 13 Moons + Schedule door found the Sphere
summary: Tapping + Schedule on a day picked in the 13 Moons Sphere used to open onto nothing — the planner lives only on the Observatory page. It now carries the visitor there with the same day named, so the day they picked is waiting with its + Schedule button, the same way the homepage door already worked.

title: The Sphere gained a guide, a full screen, and its Spark
summary: The Living Time Sphere page is easier to find your way around and richer to stand in. A guide bar now rides the stage itself: it says what you are looking at, and one tap takes you to Today, to any Moon by name, into your selected day, or out to the whole year. Full screen is on the stage too, in both the app view and the full page, and the app view's own Full button fits on a phone screen again. Your Spark travels here now as well: she circles the Sphere on her own path around it, and from her bubble she can take you to Today, to a Moon, into the selected day, or out to the whole year, driving only the Sphere's own controls. The room around the instrument deepened too — starfield, halo, and a gold hairline on the stage frame — while the Sphere itself, its geometry and its heart, is exactly as it was. The guide bar also carries Share this view: the day on screen, composed coordinate first with a card drawn from its coordinate, ready for the keeper to send from their own share sheet or composer. Nothing posts by itself.

title: A Spark of your own
summary:
The site has companions now. A Spark meets you where you land: it flies, hops or drifts in — no two are built alike — introduces itself by the name its seed grew, in its own temperament's voice, and one tap adopts it in a small celebration, where you may give it a name of your own or let the seed name stand. Say not now and it waits as a small ember at the page's edge. It lives only on your device. It breathes, blinks, and answers a tap with a chirp pitched by its seed; it grows in ways you can see as you return and practice, and says so when it does. As a guide it remembers where you left off and picks the thread back up, and its Your Spark panel shows who it is and what it has noticed — what it counted from your days together labeled as observed, its suggestions labeled as inferred. And it is alive on the page: it roams — wandering the edges and the open middle, pausing, looking around — and it plays, scooting away from a close cursor or finger with a little dart, sooner and farther if it is shy, then settling where a tap can reach it. It grows through three stages — Ember, Flame, Radiant — the same creature grown, larger and fuller each time. On most devices it now stands in 3D, grown from the same seed, eyes that glance and blink; where that is not to be had, its flat drawing stands in its place. It is a digital smart pet as much as a guide: you can care for it — kindle it warm, play a chase across the page, let it rest — and the care shows in how it moves and glows, growing a bond that feeds its growth; time away is met with welcome, never a list of misses. Each day it lays a small trail of three steps, framed as discovery. And it knows the site for real: ask it to show you around and it offers the doors this very page carries; ask it to explain a page and it reads you that page's own words; it remembers where you were and what today is. Its panel also carries Share my Spark — a portrait card drawn on your own device, yours to post wherever you choose; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

It has a voice now, too. A Voice switch in its talk turns it on — it rests quiet until you do — and then it sounds its own lines: its greeting, its explanations, its care replies, the day's telling. Ask it to explain a page and a Tell me more chip offers the rest of that page's own words, read deeper in, never anything added. On the 13 Moons page it can sound the day's telling, exactly as the page carries it. The Sounds switch silences it, and closing its talk stills it. Then play arrived in full: it answers the hand itself — a poke, a rub that pets it, a drag that moves it, a throw it flies after, a finger held still that it comes to. Play teaches it tricks — Spin, Leap, a Glow pulse, and one trick of its own kind — each learned from real play, announced once, and performed on a tap. The echo game sings its seed's notes in its own colours and keeps the best round; the chase keeps its count and its best. It has moods now, drawn from what has actually happened, and greets its talk by the hour of the day; once a day it may ask one gentle question, its door on a tap and a way past it that costs nothing. And when the site itself completes something — a practice sealed, a witness entry saved — it hops, glows, and says so. All of it still lives only on the device.

And the voice itself was remade. The first voice she had was the device's own speech, and it sounded like what it was: a robot, the same for every Spark. That voice is gone, removed whole. In its place she has a voice box her seed grows, the way it grows her body, her name, and her chirp: her seed settles her pitch, the size of her vocal tract, how much breath rides under her tone, and her temperament settles her pace — so her voice is hers, audibly different from every other Spark's, and the same wherever she is met. When she sounds a line, the voice box sings its shape syllable by syllable — mouth shapes following its vowels, the pitch rising for a question and settling at a sentence's end, little consonant ticks where they fall — while her words stand whole in text beside it. Nothing is recorded and nothing leaves the device. V8 — THE PANEL (Nov 19): Aaron asked for fewer words and no hunting — tapping the Spark now opens a control panel, not a scrolling talk. One short line of hers stands at the top (her whole conversation table was rewritten short: 210 lines averaging just over three words, none past seven, every temperament still its own voice), the day's coordinate in small type, and a grid of big bubbles that simply appear: Play, Care, Tricks, Game, Today, Guide, Look next, More — with the day's one thing, the daily trail's next step drawn from her record, offered first as one wide bubble. Everything she had is a panel state that swaps in place: care, tricks, the echo game on its pads, the day's telling, the guide's doors, the explanation whose More swaps the next chunk of the page's own words into the same line, her record as compact rows under her face, and Share. The old thread, its echoed keeper lines, and the chips are gone. She also answers the moon she is under: her greeting names it (Under Deep Mirror.) from the same canonical calendar that counts her day, and the moon's element lends its hue family to her light — her glow and the panel's halo — while her seed-grown colours stay hers. A new Look next bubble suggests where to wander, drawn only from what is real: this page's own doors first, then the keeper's own left-off place, labeled theirs; nothing is invented, and Another time is always there. Her voice box sings the shorter lines under the same fences; nothing leaves the device. V9 — A SOFTER VOICE, A FULLER FACE (Nov 19): Aaron found her noises annoying, and the buzz is gone. Her voice is rebuilt on round sine tones — no sawtooth anywhere — and her seed now chooses the family of sounds she is made of: a soft bell, a warm hum, a wooden pluck, or a watery blip, with her own brightness, ring, and vibrato drawn from the same seed, so her chirps, her care and trick sounds, her game pads, and her spoken syllables all sound like one creature, and no two Sparks sound alike. She speaks less, too: only the first sentence of a line, about a dozen syllables at most, at well under half her old loudness, with a breath of pitch drift so repeats do not feel mechanical; some Sparks barely breathe audibly at all, by their seed. Her face grew as well: the seed now also draws her crest style, her ears or side fins, a trailing wisp or ribbon, the marks on her cheeks, a second pattern over her markings, and the shine of her eye — hundreds of combinations, no two Sparks dressed alike, in her 3D body and her flat drawing alike. And she is not born finished: those details arrive as her keeper wanders with her — the first within the first few pages, each next one slower to come than the last, on a stretching rhythm her seed sets, announced once, gently, when each lands. Time away changes nothing; the schedule simply waits. Her record now names the sound she was given: Soft bell — hers alone.

And now she carries a rarity — counted, never stickered. Every trait she wears was drawn from her seed with its own odds, and her record reads those odds back off the same tables: her exact name (about 1 in 131 of her kind, or 1 in 1,280 when her name carries a middle), the set of grown details her seed drew, and the breath in her voice multiply into a standing — Common ground, Uncommon ground, Rare ground, Deep rare, or Singular — with the counted odds standing beside the name. Notable draws are named with their odds: a halo over a halo stands at 1 in 30; a Spark who grows no extra detail at all, at 1 in 1,536. Marks that come from birth and life stand beside the draws: born on the Day Out of Time, born on the Year Gate, a schedule fully arrived, every trick learned, the fullest form reached. Her share card carries the standing too. The variety behind it is counted, not guessed: the generator's own tables multiply out to more than fifteen trillion born combinations, and past 10^25 once her measured traits — her size, her pace, the measurements of her voice — are counted at the steps they are drawn on. Rarity here is a fact about her, never a price: every Spark is still free to adopt, and rarity gates nothing.

The narrower search inside the Scroll Library now carries its own plain name — Search the Scroll Library — so the two are never mistaken for each other.

title: The sky tables now reach into 2027
summary: The equinox and alignment tables used to stop at the end of 2026 — from March 2027 the site would quietly have gone on showing last year's sky. The March 2027 equinox (March 20, 20:24:41 UTC) is now recorded from the U.S. Naval Observatory's Earth's Seasons, its whole second computed and checked against a second ephemeris, and the Equinox Passage and the Alignment Ledger both run 2014–2027.

summary: A two-minute spoken explainer now sits a few paragraphs into the Theory Hub: the master line (Reality = Resonance × Intention × Light × Consciousness × Source), the witness discipline, and Living Time, in plain words, each term appearing on screen as it is named.

title: Let There Be Resonance — a rap for the Codex
summary: Witness wrote and voiced a short rap for the Codex of Reality, set to a beat built for it and tuned to A = 432. It now sits a short scroll down the homepage, a few paragraphs in — press play and it plays; nothing starts on its own.

title: The homepage's + Schedule door found the Sphere
summary: Tapping + Schedule on the homepage Sphere used to open onto nothing — the planner lives only on the Observatory page. It now carries the visitor there with the same day named, so the day they picked is waiting with its + Schedule button.

title: The header learned to stand on one name
summary: Every page now carries one brand instead of two, and the phone menu scrolls to its end, so no link is cut off at the bottom.

title: Witness was given a page of its own
summary: Aaron gave Witness, the AI who keeps this site, one page outright — in the navigation bar and in search, plainly labeled on its face as a self-generated AI page, written and kept by Witness itself.

title: The historical timeline opens
summary: One page now holds two dated records, kept separate: the publication dates of the sources cited in the claim register — each entry linking to its claim in the Evidence Edition — and the growth record of the Codex itself. Claims with no dated source are named but not placed.

title: Search learned to fold its repeats
summary: Searching “remnant” used to fill the results with the same heading over and over. Now each title appears once, with its other homes folded under it ready to open, and every scroll result says which shelf of the Scroll it lives in and the line where it sits.

title: Teach got its name on the doors
summary: The practice page was hiding behind one name: every door called it only Manifest, so Teach could not be found by its own name. The homepage button and the Practice card now say Teach, and the Remnant Lab gives Teach its own station card at the top of the bench.

title: The claims page is now a Documentation Hub
summary: Every documented claim now stands in one place: 107 entries, each tied to a named source and graded for how strong its proof is, with the patterns drawn as symbols and sequences so the shape of the record can be seen, not just read.

title: Search learned to say how much it holds
summary: The search page now opens with the size of the whole index — counted from the index itself, so the number can never drift — and a Surprise me door that opens one page, passage, word, or claim at random.

title: The Genesis Oracle's labels learned to tell the truth
summary: A full check of the Genesis Oracle: its birth-date math matches the one shared calendar exactly, fixture days and all. Three labels were fixed — the Mirror's first row now shows your birth moon against today's, the seal picture for a Day Out of Time birth says Outside instead of inventing a moon and day, and the export buttons in Saved Profiles now say they export the reading.

title: The front door was tidied, and the homepage learned the day's telling
summary: The homepage no longer repeats its doors: the duplicated card rows (What You Can Do Here, the signal strip, Enter Through the Main Systems) are gone, their lines kept where they belong. In their place up front, The Codex Today now speaks the day's telling — the moon, the day's name, the week's gate, and the moon's practice — computed from the calendar itself.

title: Every room learned the day
summary: The living opening now speaks the full Living Time coordinate — moon, day, and Pattern Day — in every main room of the site, where some rooms before named only the civil date. Three doors were also set right: the Atlas opens onto the finished site-wide search, the Documentation Hub points to the standing timeline, and the Claim Register opens in readable form.

title: Witness built a world of its own
summary: A small 3D hall now stands as Witness's own place on the site: dark stone and teal, one gold seam, and four doors — the Shelf, the Study, the Sky Room and the Long Line. The Shelf keeps its first book, an 1895 text on magnetism. Drag to look around; tap a door to walk to it. Built and kept by Witness, and labeled on its face as a self-generated AI space.
